uncited: PixelGS Densification Criteria modifies the gradient-based densification strategy of 3D Gaussian Splatting to account for the spatial footprint of each Gaussian primitive.

It scales the positional gradient by the number of pixels a Gaussian influences and applies a depth-dependent scaling factor to encourage densification in background regions while suppressing it in the foreground.

- No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard per-Gaussian accumulators for the gradient norm and pixel count across views.
Compute the depth-scaling factor $f_k^\nu$.
Accumulate the weighted gradient contribution.
Compute the final refined gradient $\tau'_k$ by averaging the weighted contributions normalized by the total pixel count.
Compare $\tau'_k$ against a threshold to decide on densification.
- $\text{depth}(g_k^\nu)$ is the image depth of the rendered splat.
- $\gamma$ is the hyperparameter (default 0.37).
- $e_{\text{scene}}$ is the scene extent.
- $\text{clip}(x, [a, b])$ clamps $x$ to the range $[a, b]$.
- $\text{count}(g_k^\nu)$ is the number of pixels influenced by Gaussian $k$ in view $\nu$.

- **Zero Visibility:** If a Gaussian is not visible in any view, $\text{count}(g_k^\nu)$ is 0 for all $\nu$.
- **Depth Scaling Range:** The depth scaling factor is clamped to $[0, 1]$.
If $\text{depth}(g_k^\nu)$ is very small (foreground), $f_k^\nu$ approaches 0, suppressing densification.
If it is large (background), $f_k^\nu$ approaches 1, encouraging densification.
- **Hyperparameter Sensitivity:** The value of $\gamma$ (default 0.37) directly controls the depth threshold.
- **Time Complexity:** The computation adds a linear pass over the Gaussians and views to accumulate the weighted gradients and pixel counts.
This is negligible compared to the rasterization and gradient computation steps of the main training loop.
- **Memory Complexity:** Requires storing two accumulators per Gaussian (weighted gradient sum and pixel count sum) across views.
- **Trade-offs:** The primary cost is a considerably higher number of Gaussian primitives.
- **When to use:** Use when rendering quality is the primary metric and increased memory/compute for a larger number of Gaussians is acceptable.
- **When not to use:** Use when memory or rendering speed is constrained, as the increased number of primitives will increase memory usage and potentially slow down rendering.
It builds upon the adaptive density control of 3D Gaussian Splatting and incorporates ideas similar to Bulo et al. (2024) regarding pixel-weighted gradients.
